items.question: What distinguishes a personal health record from the other record types discussed this week?
options: The patient controls or maintains it and may connect it to provider systems
Hospitals produce it only for patients who have been discharged
It contains only information entered by clinicians during visits
It is stored on the patient's phone and can never be shared
items.rationale: A personal health record is defined by who controls it: the individual maintains it, decides what it contains, and may connect it to provider systems. It is not limited to discharge summaries, it is not clinician-authored, and it can certainly be shared; control by the person is the distinguishing feature.

items.question: A group practice keeps scanned records in one system and clinical data in four specialty systems that do not exchange information. How should you classify it?
options: A single electronic health record, because every record is electronic
A clinical data warehouse serving the whole practice
A collection of electronic medical records plus a document repository
A personal health record, because patients can request copies
items.rationale: Each specialty system serves one department and does not exchange information, which is the boundary that defines an EMR, and the scanned archive holds images rather than structured data, which makes it a document repository. Being electronic does not make a system an EHR, and patient copies do not make it a PHR.

items.question: A patient's uploaded home blood pressure readings arrive without a device name or units. What is the most important first step?
options: Enter the readings into the vital signs flowsheet as clinical values
Discard the readings because they cannot be trusted
Ask the patient to stop using the portal for readings
Label them as patient-reported with source and verification status before anyone acts on them
items.rationale: Patient-generated data is valuable, but its provenance must travel with it. Labeling the readings with their source, units when known, and a verification status preserves patient control while preventing an unverified number from being treated as a clinical measurement. Discarding the data or entering it as verified both destroy information.

items.question: An abnormal laboratory result has been finalized and appears in the chart, but no one has opened it. Which core function has not yet finished its work?
options: Order management, because the order was never actually placed
Results management, because the result has not reached a reviewer who acts on it
Administrative processes, because the visit has not been billed
Health information and data, because the value is not stored
items.rationale: Results management covers the whole lifecycle from final result through review, communication, and follow-up, so a final but unopened result means the function is only half complete. The order clearly was placed, the value is stored, and billing is unrelated to whether the patient was told.

items.question: A hospital reports the highest possible maturity score and asks whether it can stop auditing result follow-up. What should you recommend?
options: Stop auditing, because the score demonstrates that the workflow is safe
Audit only the departments that scored lowest on the model
Keep auditing, because the score reflects adopted capabilities rather than local performance
Replace the audit with an annual clinician satisfaction survey
items.rationale: A maturity score is a structured assessment of adopted capabilities and governance; it does not measure whether a specific closed loop, such as result follow-up, actually closes for each patient. Local evidence must confirm performance, so the audit continues, and the score is used to decide which loops deserve the closest look.

items.question: In the practice chart, the audit history for a result shows created at 09:14, finalized at 10:02, and no viewed entry. What does this evidence support?
options: The result was reviewed but the audit log failed to record it
The result exists and is final but has not been opened by anyone
The order was never placed, so the result is an error
The patient was notified of the result at 10:02
items.rationale: Audit evidence supports exactly what it records: a result was created, then finalized, and no view event exists. Assuming a silent log failure or a patient notification adds facts the evidence does not contain, and a finalized result cannot exist without an order, so the honest reading is final and unopened.

weeks.title: How an EHR is built: systems, sources, and chart sections

items.question: According to information systems theory, which set of components makes up a health information system?
options: Hardware and software only
Servers, networks, and databases
Hardware, software, and people, policy, and process
The EHR vendor's modules and their interfaces
items.rationale: Houser defines an information system as hardware, software, and a human element (people, policy, process) working toward a common purpose. The other options leave out the human layer, where most failures occur.

items.question: A nurse notices that the potassium in the EHR shows 5.9 but the lab called a corrected value of 4.8 an hour ago. Where should the analyst look first?
options: The EHR's display settings
The interface: whether the correction message was sent and filed
The nurse's documentation in the flowsheet
The physician's inbox rules
items.rationale: The LIS is the source system. If it holds a corrected value but the EHR does not, the correction message did not arrive or did not file. The interface log is the first evidence to check.

items.question: Which of the following is an example of structured (discrete) data?
options: A pain score of 7 entered in the flowsheet pain row
A nurse's narrative note describing the patient's mood
A scanned referral letter from an outside cardiologist
An audio recording of a telehealth visit
items.rationale: A flowsheet row stores a defined value the computer can graph, alert on, and report. The others are unstructured: text, images, or audio that people can read but computers cannot easily use.

items.question: A patient's penicillin allergy appears only in a scanned outside record. A penicillin-class antibiotic is ordered. What is the most likely result?
options: A drug–allergy alert fires because the allergy is in the chart
The interface engine flags the order
The pharmacy system blocks the order automatically
No alert fires because the allergy is not stored as structured data
items.rationale: Decision support runs on structured data. An allergy that exists only in a scanned document is invisible to the alert logic. This is why allergy reconciliation into the coded allergy list matters.

items.question: What is the main job of an interface engine?
options: Store the patient's longitudinal record
Display results to clinicians
Route, translate, and log messages between systems
Generate clinical decision support alerts
items.rationale: An interface engine sits between systems, routing messages, translating codes and formats, and logging traffic. Storage is the repository's job; display and alerts are the EHR's.

items.question: A quality dashboard shows yesterday's sepsis bundle compliance but none of today's cases. What best explains this?
options: The EHR is malfunctioning
The data warehouse is loaded overnight from the repository
Sepsis cases are stored as unstructured data
Today's nurses have not documented yet
items.rationale: Warehouses are typically refreshed on a schedule, often nightly, so reports lag the live repository. That lag is by design, not a malfunction.

items.question: Which statement best distinguishes a clinical data repository from a clinical data warehouse?
options: The repository supports real-time care for one patient; the warehouse supports analysis across many patients
The repository is for billing; the warehouse is for care
The repository is cloud-based; the warehouse is on-premises
They are two names for the same database
items.rationale: The repository is optimized for fast, current, single-patient access during care. The warehouse holds copies reorganized for population queries and reporting.

items.question: In the DIKW continuum, 'Marcus's potassium is 6.2 mmol/L and flagged high' is an example of:
options: Data
Wisdom
Knowledge
Information
items.rationale: A value with units, a reference range, and a patient is information. Knowledge would connect it to what we know (ACE inhibitor, arrhythmia risk); wisdom is the right action.

items.question: A hospital moves its EHR to vendor hosting. Which responsibility shifts most directly to the vendor?
options: Deciding which order sets clinicians use
Training nurses on documentation
Running and patching the servers and meeting uptime commitments
Approving clinical content changes
items.rationale: Hosting moves infrastructure operations (servers, patches, uptime) to the vendor under a contract. Clinical content, governance, and training remain the organization's responsibility.

items.question: The July 2024 CrowdStrike outage disrupted hospital care even where EHR servers were running. Why?
options: EHR vendors used CrowdStrike to store patient data
Workstations clinicians use to reach the EHR crashed
The outage deleted EHR databases
HL7 interfaces were shut down by regulators
items.rationale: The faulty update crashed Windows computers, including the workstations clinicians use. The EHR can be healthy while the devices people use to reach it are not, which is why downtime planning must include endpoints.

items.question: A nurse proposes changing a required field in the admission assessment. According to good governance, what should happen first?
options: The request is triaged and reviewed by the appropriate clinical council
The analyst builds it in the live system that afternoon
The vendor is asked to add it to the next upgrade
The nurse manager emails all staff about the change
items.rationale: Changes are triaged and approved by the right governance body before build, because a change that helps one unit may affect others. Building directly in production skips testing.

items.question: Which SDLC phase most directly would have caught a mismatch between the reference lab's critical flag (6.5) and hospital policy (6.0)?
options: Planning
Implementation
Maintenance
Testing
items.rationale: Testing with realistic scenarios, such as a potassium of 6.2, would show the result arriving as 'H' rather than critical. Analysis can identify requirements, but testing is where the mismatch becomes visible before go-live.

items.question: In health IT (as opposed to general systems theory), a 'closed system' usually means:
options: A system with no feedback loops
A system that is offline during downtime
Proprietary technology that is not freely shared with others
A system that only clinicians can access
items.rationale: Houser notes that in health IT, 'closed' refers to proprietary technology, while 'open' refers to standards-based systems that can interconnect.

items.question: Marcus Reed's critical potassium went unseen over a weekend. Which fix addresses the root cause rather than a symptom?
options: Remind physicians to check their inbox more often
Create inbox coverage rules and route unacknowledged critical results to the on-call clinician
Add a second pop-up alert for high potassium
Discipline the physician who ordered the test
items.rationale: The root cause was routing: results went to an unavailable person with no coverage. Coverage rules plus escalation fix the pathway. Reminders, extra alerts, and discipline target individuals and tend not to last.

items.question: Which chart section most commonly causes useless alerts when data is entered incorrectly, for example logging nausea from codeine as a 'drug allergy'?
options: Allergy list
Problem list
Flowsheets
Demographics
items.rationale: Intolerances recorded as allergies generate drug–allergy alerts that clinicians learn to override, which contributes to alert fatigue. Accurate allergy type and reaction data make alerts meaningful.

items.question: Sittig and Singh's sociotechnical model is most useful for which purpose?
options: Calculating EHR return on investment
Designing HL7 interface messages
Choosing between Epic and Oracle Health
Showing that health IT problems usually span several dimensions such as workflow, people, and policy
items.rationale: The model's eight dimensions show why health IT problems rarely have a single technical cause. It is an analysis tool, not a financial or technical design method.

weeks.title: The front door: identity, scheduling, registration, and coding

items.question: What is the primary purpose of a master patient index (MPI)?
options: To store every clinical note and result for each patient
To verify insurance eligibility before each visit
To assign ICD-10-CM codes to each registered patient
To identify each person and link all of the record numbers that belong to them
items.rationale: The MPI is the organization's index of people: identifying details plus every record number linked to that person. Notes and results live in the clinical repository; coding and eligibility are separate functions.

items.question: An ED nurse opens the chart of a 34-year-old man and sees a prior hysterectomy and a blood type that differs from today's lab result. Which identity problem is most likely?
options: A duplicate record
An interface delay from the lab
An overlay: two people's information in one record
A coding error on the problem list
items.rationale: Clinical facts that cannot belong to this patient, like a hysterectomy on a male chart and a conflicting blood type, point to an overlay, where two people share one record. A duplicate hides information rather than adding a stranger's.

items.question: Which statement best describes a duplicate medical record?
options: Two different patients whose information was combined into one record
One patient with two or more records in the same system
A copy of the record sent to another hospital through an HIE
A backup copy of the record kept for downtime
items.rationale: A duplicate is one person with more than one record in the same system, which splits their history. Two people in one record is an overlay; copies sent through exchange or kept for downtime are not duplicates in the MPI sense.

items.question: A caller says she is Liu Huang. The search returns 'Liu Huang' and 'Liu H.' with the same birth date and different phone numbers. What should the scheduler do?
options: Confirm additional identifiers with the caller, book on the verified record, and send the pair to the HIM identity queue
Book on whichever record appears first in the search results
Merge the two records because the birth dates match
Create a new record to avoid choosing the wrong one
items.rationale: Front-desk staff verify identity with the patient and escalate possible duplicates; authorized HIM staff decide on merges. Merging on a shared birth date risks an overlay, and creating a new record adds another duplicate.

items.question: Which description fits deterministic patient matching?
options: Records are linked using a national patient identifier
Each identifier receives a weight and the weights are added into a score
A human reviews every possible match before linking
Records are linked only when selected identifiers match exactly
items.rationale: Deterministic matching uses exact-match rules on chosen fields. Weighted scoring is probabilistic matching; human review is a step for uncertain pairs; the US has no national patient identifier.

items.question: A probabilistic matching engine scores a pair of records between its 'automatic link' and 'new person' thresholds. What should happen next?
options: Link them automatically, since the score is above zero
Discard the lower-scoring record
Send the pair to a human reviewer, typically in HIM, for a documented decision
Create a third record to hold the uncertain data
items.rationale: The gray zone between thresholds exists precisely so that a trained person can compare identifiers and decide. Automatic linking risks overlays; discarding or creating records loses or fragments history.

items.question: An organization lowers its automatic-merge threshold so that more pairs link without review. What is the most likely consequence?
options: Fewer duplicates and fewer overlays
Fewer duplicates, but more overlays
More duplicates, but fewer overlays
No change, because the threshold only affects billing
items.rationale: A lower bar links more pairs automatically, which clears likely duplicates but also merges some different people, creating overlays. Thresholds trade one error for the other; they rarely reduce both.

items.question: Twin brothers share a last name, birth date, address, and phone number. Their first names differ by one letter (Jaden and Jayden). How should registration handle them?
options: Treat them as two people, and add a 'similar name' or twin alert to both charts
Merge them, because four identifiers match
Keep only the record with more visits
Let the matching algorithm decide without review
items.rationale: Twins share almost every household identifier, so matching software tends to overrate them as one person. The right move is to keep separate records, confirm with distinguishing identifiers, and add an alert.

items.question: What do the ASC X12 270 and 271 transactions do?
options: Send a claim and receive payment
Request a prior authorization and receive an appeal decision
Send a lab order and receive the result
Ask an insurer whether a patient's coverage is active and receive its answer
items.rationale: The 270 is an eligibility inquiry and the 271 is the insurer's response. Claims, lab messages, and prior authorization use other transactions.

items.question: A Medicaid patient's insurance card was scanned last month. She returns today. What should the front desk do about coverage?
options: Nothing; the card on file is sufficient
Ask the patient to sign a form saying her coverage has not changed
Run an eligibility check for today's date of service
Bill the patient directly to avoid delays
items.rationale: Coverage can change monthly, especially for Medicaid, so eligibility is verified for each date of service. A card on file is a starting point, not verification.

items.question: A clinic's no-show rate rose to 14%. Which change is most likely to help without cutting access for patients who do show up?
options: Double-book every slot for all providers
Automated reminders with easy rescheduling, plus a wait list that backfills canceled slots
Remove all same-day slots from the template
Require a deposit for every appointment
items.rationale: Reminders reduce missed visits, and wait-list backfill turns cancellations into care. Blanket double-booking overloads clinicians; removing same-day slots and deposits reduce access for the patients who need it.

items.question: In Adelman's trial, requiring prescribers to re-enter a patient's initials, sex, and age reduced wrong-patient orders by 41%, while a click-through ID alert reduced them by 16%. What is the best interpretation?
options: Active confirmation is more effective than a passive click, but it costs time, so it should target high-risk moments
Alerts never work and should be removed
Wrong-patient orders are too rare to be worth addressing
The results show that registration is the only source of wrong-patient errors
items.rationale: The re-entry step forced attention and worked better, but it added about 6.6 seconds per session. The design lesson is to use active confirmation where the risk justifies the time, not everywhere.

items.question: Which statement correctly separates ICD-10-CM from CPT?
options: ICD-10-CM is used only for mortality statistics; CPT is used for all billing
ICD-10-CM describes the service performed; CPT describes the diagnosis
Both describe diagnoses, but CPT is used only in hospitals
ICD-10-CM describes the diagnosis or reason for the visit; CPT describes the service performed
items.rationale: ICD-10-CM classifies diagnoses and reasons for care (why); CPT codes the services clinicians perform (what). Both appear on claims, linked so each service points to a justifying diagnosis.

items.question: Dr. Chen's note says 'bursitis of the right shoulder'. Which diagnosis code does the documentation support?
options: M75.52 Bursitis of left shoulder
M75.50 Bursitis of unspecified shoulder
M75.51 Bursitis of right shoulder
99213 Office visit, established patient
items.rationale: ICD-10-CM carries laterality, and the note specifies the right side, so M75.51 is supported. The unspecified code discards documented detail, the left-side code contradicts the note, and 99213 is a CPT service code, not a diagnosis.

items.question: A clinic visit takes place on October 6, 2026. Which ICD-10-CM code set applies?
options: The FY2026 set, because the fiscal year has not yet ended
The FY2027 set, which took effect October 1, 2026
Whichever set the clinic's pick list last loaded
ICD-11, which replaced ICD-10-CM in 2026
items.rationale: ICD-10-CM updates take effect each October 1, the start of the federal fiscal year, so the FY2027 set applies to dates of service from October 1, 2026. The US has not adopted ICD-11.

items.question: Which terminology is designed to identify laboratory tests and clinical observations such as vital signs?
options: LOINC
CPT
HCPCS Level II
ICD-10-PCS
items.rationale: LOINC names tests and observations so results from different labs can be recognized as the same test. CPT and HCPCS code services and supplies for billing; ICD-10-PCS codes inpatient procedures.

items.question: A health system turns on AI-assisted coding that suggests codes from clinical documentation. Which safeguard best addresses the main risk?
options: Let the AI submit all claims automatically to reduce delays
Turn off the claim scrubber, since the AI replaces it
Train nurses to document less so the AI has less to read
Audit a sample of AI-suggested codes against the documentation and track error types, with humans confirming codes before submission
items.rationale: Computer-assisted coding depends on documentation quality, so the key safeguards are human confirmation and ongoing audits comparing codes to the record. Fully automatic submission and removing checks remove oversight; less documentation lowers accuracy.

items.question: A clinic's claims are being denied for 'patient not eligible' and 'member ID not found'. Where in the revenue cycle should the analyst look first?
options: The coding step, for incorrect CPT codes
The payment posting step in the billing office
The front end: registration, identity matching, and eligibility checks
The clinicians' documentation templates
items.rationale: Eligibility and member ID denials trace to registration: wrong or duplicate patient records, outdated coverage, or no eligibility check on the date of service. Coding and documentation errors produce different denial reasons.

weeks.title: Medication, orders, results, and clinical decision support

items.question: In closed-loop medication management, which step comes between the prescriber entering the order in CPOE and the medication being dispensed?
options: Pharmacist review and verification of the order
Barcode scanning at the bedside
Documentation on the eMAR
Medication reconciliation at discharge
items.rationale: After the prescriber enters the order, a pharmacist reviews it for interactions, allergies, and dosing before it is dispensed. Scanning and eMAR documentation happen at administration; reconciliation happens at transitions of care.

items.question: Barcode medication administration is designed to verify which set of 'rights' at the bedside?
options: Right patient, medication, dose, allergy, and indication
Right information, person, format, channel, and time
Right patient, diagnosis, dose, prescriber, and pharmacy
Right patient, medication, dose, time, and route
items.rationale: Barcode scanning checks the five rights of medication administration: patient, medication, dose, time, and route. The information-person-format-channel-time list is the CDS five rights, a different framework for designing decision support.

items.question: On 4 West, several nurses are scanning wristbands taped to the workstation because patients' bands often won't scan. What is the best informatics response?
options: Remind staff in writing that workarounds violate policy and will be disciplined
Turn off the wristband scan requirement on 4 West until the problem resolves
Investigate why bands fail to scan, fix the cause with the owners, and audit how scans happen
Add a pop-up reminding nurses to scan the patient, not the cart
items.rationale: Workarounds signal a system problem. Finding and fixing the cause (printer, band stock, scanner settings) removes the reason for the workaround, and auditing how scans happen shows whether it worked. Discipline alone drives workarounds underground, turning off scanning removes the safety check, and another pop-up adds alert burden.

items.question: A nurse scans Sofia Petrov's wristband and a potassium chloride tablet. The order was verified by pharmacy, and the scan beeps green. Which error can barcode scanning still NOT catch?
options: The tablet belongs to the patient in the next bed
The order itself is unsafe because her potassium is already high
The tablet is 40 mEq but the order is 20 mEq
The dose is being given four hours early
items.rationale: Scanning compares the barcodes to an active, verified order. It catches wrong patient, wrong dose, and wrong time, but it cannot judge whether the order itself is clinically appropriate. That judgment belongs to the prescriber, the pharmacist, CDS, and the nurse's own review of labs.

items.question: In a clinical decision support system, which component applies rules to a patient's data to decide whether to show an alert?
options: The inference (rules) engine
The user interface
The knowledge base
The clinical data warehouse
items.rationale: The inference or rules engine evaluates patient-specific data against rules drawn from the knowledge base. The knowledge base stores the evidence and rules; the user interface presents the result to the clinician.

items.question: Marcus Reed's potassium of 5.7 is final at 10:02. Dr. Chen acknowledges it in her inbox at 10:30. There is no task and no documented patient contact. What is the state of this result?
options: Closed: the ordering clinician has reviewed it
Closed, because the result is visible to the patient in the portal
Pending: the result is not final until acknowledged
Reviewed but not closed: the patient has not been told and no follow-up has an owner
items.rationale: Acknowledgment shows the clinician saw the value. The loop closes when the patient has been informed and the next step has a named owner and date. Portal visibility is not the same as communication or a plan.

items.question: Patients at a Fordham clinic are reading abnormal results in the portal at night, before anyone calls. Which change best fits current rules and good practice?
options: Hold all abnormal results for seven days until a clinician reviews them
Stop portal notifications for lab results
Keep releasing results promptly, add plain-language result comments, and set up a nurse outreach pathway for abnormal values
Release only normal results automatically and print abnormal ones for mailing
items.rationale: Information blocking rules generally expect prompt release, with narrow exceptions. The safer path is workflow: plain-language comments, proactive outreach for abnormal values, and messages routed to someone working. Blanket delays or selective release conflict with patients' access rights.

items.question: According to Houser, what distinguishes passive CDS advice from active advice?
options: Passive advice is less accurate than active advice
Passive advice is available when the user seeks it and does not interrupt the workflow
Passive advice is shown only to pharmacists
Passive advice is generated by machine learning rather than rules
items.rationale: Passive advice, such as reference material or a list column, is there when the user looks; active advice is pushed at a trigger and interrupts. Accuracy, audience, and the method behind the rule are separate questions.

items.question: A correct renal-dosing alert fires as a pop-up to the medical assistant at check-in, before any medication has been ordered. Which of the CDS five rights does it fail most clearly?
options: Right person and right time
Right information, because the creatinine is wrong
Right format, because it should be in bold text
Right channel, because it should be sent by text page
items.rationale: The information is correct, but it reaches someone who cannot change a dose, before the decision is being made. Retargeting it to the prescriber at the moment of ordering fixes the person and the time. Format and channel changes alone would not help.

items.question: A weekly report shows the duplicate-therapy alert for acetaminophen fired 1,204 times, was overridden 97% of the time, and changed the order 1% of the time. Most cases come from two admission order sets that each include acetaminophen. What is the best first action?
options: Convert it to a hard stop so prescribers must cancel one order
Retrain prescribers to read duplicate-therapy alerts
Leave it: overrides are quick and the alert is technically correct
With pharmacy and nursing, fix the order sets and retire or narrow the alert, relying on a cumulative maximum-dose check
items.rationale: The data show a low-value interruption with a known upstream cause. Fixing the order-set defaults and replacing the alert with a cumulative dose check keeps the safety goal while removing noise. A hard stop adds burden, training doesn't change the design, and leaving it feeds alert fatigue.

items.question: In Knake's NICU study, a pop-up for PICC dressing changes was acted on 1.7% of the time. After it became a column on the nurses' patient list, overdue changes fell from 22% to 8%. What best explains why the passive design worked here?
options: Passive alerts are always more effective than interruptive ones
Nurses were disciplined for overdue dressing changes during the study
The information appeared in the channel and at the time nurses plan their work, so it fit the workflow
The dressing-change policy was relaxed so fewer changes were due
items.rationale: The team observed the real workflow and put the information where nurses already look when planning care: right format, channel, and time. Earlier research found passive alerts often ignored, so passive is not automatically better; fit to workflow is what mattered.

items.question: Why does Houser emphasize that prescribers should enter orders into CPOE themselves rather than having a scribe or nurse enter them?
options: Direct entry is required for billing
So the person making the decision sees and responds to decision support at the moment of ordering
Because scribes are not allowed to use the EHR
Because orders entered by nurses cannot be verified by pharmacy
items.rationale: CDS delivers value when the alert reaches the person who can change the order. When someone else enters it, the alert goes to the wrong person. This is the 'right person' principle applied to CPOE.

items.question: Under DEA rules for electronic prescribing of controlled substances (EPCS), what must be in place before a prescriber can sign an opioid prescription electronically?
options: Identity proofing and two-factor authentication for signing
A faxed paper copy signed in ink
Verbal confirmation from the pharmacist
A signed patient consent in the portal
items.rationale: EPCS requires verified prescriber identity and strong authentication (two factors) with a digital certificate, as described in Chapter 9. Fax, verbal confirmation, and patient consent are not the security controls the rules require.

items.question: While Dr. Patel e-prescribes, the screen shows that a brand-name drug will cost Elena Garcia $85 at her pharmacy and a generic alternative $4. What is this tool and its main purpose?
options: Drug–drug interaction checking, to prevent adverse events
Formulary substitution by the pharmacy after the prescription is sent
Electronic prior authorization, to submit paperwork to the payer
Real-time prescription benefit, to show patient-specific cost and coverage while the choice can still change
items.rationale: Real-time prescription benefit returns the patient's cost and coverage at the chosen pharmacy during ordering, so the prescriber and patient can pick an affordable option and adherence improves. Prior authorization and pharmacy substitution happen at different steps.

items.question: An ambient AI tool drafts 'potassium chloride 20 mEq daily' for Marcus Reed, whose potassium is 5.7, and the clinician signs the whole draft queue in one click. Which safeguard matters most?
options: Auto-sign AI drafts when the model's confidence is high
Let nurses release AI-drafted orders to save clinician time
Keep AI drafts pending and clearly labeled, run them through the same CDS, and block bulk signing of high-risk drugs
Turn off CDS for AI-drafted orders to reduce alert fatigue
items.rationale: AI will make some errors, so the human signature has to be a real review. Labeling, pending status, full CDS checks, and no bulk signing of high-risk drugs keep the clinician as the decision maker. The other options remove or weaken checks.

items.question: The heart failure admission order set pre-checks scheduled acetaminophen, and the pneumonia set pre-checks PRN acetaminophen. Prescribers using both get duplicate alerts on almost every admission. Where is the best fix?
options: In the alert: suppress all duplicate-therapy alerts hospital-wide
In the order sets: align the defaults through governance so they don't conflict
In training: teach prescribers to uncheck one of them
In pharmacy: have pharmacists discontinue one order at verification
items.rationale: The alert is a symptom of conflicting defaults. Fixing the order sets through governance removes the duplicates at the source. Suppressing all duplicate alerts removes a useful check elsewhere, and training or pharmacy cleanup leaves the flawed default in place.

items.question: Which statement best describes alert fatigue?
options: Clinicians become desensitized after many low-value alerts and start dismissing important ones too
Computers slow down when too many alerts run at once
Patients become anxious after seeing many abnormal results
Pharmacists refuse to verify orders that triggered alerts
items.rationale: Alert fatigue is desensitization from frequent, often irrelevant alerts, which leads clinicians to override or overlook important ones. It is a human response to system design, not a hardware or patient issue.

items.question: Which list best describes the purposes that clinical documentation serves at the same time?
options: Billing and regulatory compliance, with care as a side benefit
Patient care, team communication, billing, and legal evidence
Storing data for the EHR vendor's analytics
Proving to managers that nurses completed assigned tasks
items.rationale: A single note supports the next clinician's care, communication across the team, billing for the service, and legal evidence of what happened. Treating billing or compliance as the main purpose is how notes become long and defensive.

items.question: A nurse documents a Braden score of 12 in the flowsheet row, and a colleague writes 'high risk for skin breakdown' in a narrative note. Which entry can automatically trigger the pressure-injury prevention order set?
options: The Braden score in the flowsheet row, because it's a structured value a rule can evaluate
The narrative note, because it states the risk in words
Both equally, because the EHR reads all documentation
Neither, because order sets can only be triggered by physicians
items.rationale: Decision support runs on structured values in defined fields. A rule can evaluate a Braden score below a threshold; it can't reliably interpret a sentence in a narrative note.

items.question: According to Houser, what is 'note bloat'?
options: Clinical notes that are longer because patients have more diagnoses
Notes that include too many structured flowsheet values
The storage cost of keeping notes in the EHR database
Records cluttered with unnecessary or irrelevant copied detail that makes key information hard to find
items.rationale: Houser describes copy-and-paste convenience leading to note bloat: records filled with unnecessary detail that obscures pertinent data and can harm patient safety.

items.question: An admission skin assessment template pre-fills 'Skin: intact' for every patient. What is the safest redesign?
options: Keep the default and add a banner reminding nurses to check the skin
Remove the skin row so nurses document skin in a narrative note
Default the row to 'not assessed' and require the nurse to select a finding
Lock the template so the default can't be changed without IT
items.rationale: A neutral default records nothing until the nurse acts, so the finding reflects an actual assessment. A reminder banner leaves the false default in place, and removing the row loses structured data.

items.question: Sofia Petrov's sacral skin row shows 'intact' carried forward for four shifts while her Braden score falls; a stage 2 injury is then found. Which fix addresses the root cause?
options: Retrain all 4 West nurses on skin assessment and leave the flowsheet unchanged
Block carry-forward on skin rows and require a fresh skin assessment when Braden drops
Remove the Braden score because it didn't prevent the injury
Require a narrative skin note every shift in addition to the flowsheet
items.rationale: The build made copying the fastest path and never linked the falling Braden score to a fresh look. Blocking carry-forward on rows that need reassessment and triggering one on risk change fixes the design. Retraining alone doesn't change the path of least resistance.

items.question: A study of 104 million notes found about half of all words were duplicated from earlier documentation, across physicians, nurses, and therapists. Which conclusion is most defensible?
options: Duplication is widespread and adaptive, so the fix is safer design and review rather than a ban alone
Clinicians are careless and should be disciplined for copying
Duplicated text is harmless because it was accurate when first written
Only physician notes need copy-forward controls
items.rationale: Duplication that common across every role signals a system that asks people to re-document the same things. Bans tend to produce workarounds; safer design (source tags, blocked rows, review) addresses the cause. Copied text can become stale and wrong.

items.question: In Hendrich's 36-hospital time-and-motion study of medical-surgical nurses, which activity took the largest share of nursing practice time?
options: Direct patient care activities
Medication administration
Care coordination
Documentation
items.rationale: Documentation took about 35% of nursing practice time, more than care coordination (about 21%), patient care activities (about 19%), or medication administration (about 17%).

items.question: 4 West's practice council wants to cut nursing documentation time this quarter. Which first step best reflects documentation-burden reduction work such as AMIA's 25x5?
options: Purchase an ambient AI tool and let it fill the flowsheet
Ask nurses to chart faster by batching at the end of the shift
Inventory flowsheet rows and retire those no one uses for care, quality, or regulation
Add a new required field so nurses can report their documentation time
items.rationale: Removing documentation that adds no value is the cheapest and safest relief, and it should come before automating the rest. Batching at shift end harms timeliness, and new required fields add burden.

items.question: Nurses on a unit resist point-of-care charting because they feel it intrudes on patients, and they prefer charting at the station. According to Houser's process-improvement guidance, what is the best approach?
options: Mandate bedside charting because it is always more accurate
Examine the implications of each option with the nurses and consider alternatives such as charting stations placed throughout the unit
Keep station charting because nurses prefer it
Let each nurse choose without measuring the effect
items.rationale: Houser notes that neither option is inherently right. The team should understand the implications of each and may find a middle path, such as charting kiosks placed throughout the unit, that improves timeliness without intruding.

items.question: According to CMS guidance, what must an amendment to a signed medical record include?
options: A clear label as an amendment, the date and author, and the original content preserved
A replacement of the original text so the record reads correctly
Only the date, as long as it's made within 24 hours
Approval from the health information management department before it's entered
items.rationale: CMS requires amendments, corrections, and delayed entries to be clearly identified as such, show the date and author, and leave all original content visible. CMS sets no fixed deadline, though very late entries invite scrutiny.

items.question: Dr. Chen signed Liu Huang's note at 10:40. At 14:05 she notices the assessment says 'left shoulder' although the exam documented the right. What should she do?
options: Reopen the signed note, change 'left' to 'right', and re-sign
Delete the note and write a new one with the correct side
Leave it, because the exam section already shows the correct side
Add a dated, signed amendment giving the correction and the reason, leaving the original visible
items.rationale: Signed notes are corrected by amendment: dated, attributed, with a reason, and with the original preserved. Editing or deleting a signed note destroys the record of what was relied on. Leaving the error lets it flow into coding and future notes.

items.question: At 23:00 a nurse realizes she performed a neuro check at 19:00 but never documented it. What is the correct approach?
options: Leave it undocumented, because a missed entry can't be fixed
Backdate the entry to 19:00 so the flowsheet looks complete
Enter it now as a late entry, timed now, stating that the check was performed at 19:00
Ask the oncoming nurse to document it at the next check
items.rationale: A late entry records care that really happened, entered at the current time with a clear reference to when it occurred. Backdating misrepresents when documentation was created, and having someone else document it breaks authorship.

items.question: A resident's note includes a detailed abdominal exam. The attending did not examine the patient but co-signs with 'I have seen and examined the patient and agree with the resident's findings.' What is the main integrity problem?
options: Co-signature is not allowed on resident notes
The attestation claims work the attending didn't do, so the signed record is inaccurate
The resident should have written the exam in the plan section
There is no problem, because the resident's exam was documented
items.rationale: Attestation makes the signer accountable for what it states. Claiming to have examined the patient when no exam happened creates a false record, with legal and billing consequences, even if the resident's own exam was accurate.

items.question: Since the 2021 AMA and CMS changes, how is the level of an office evaluation and management (E/M) visit determined?
options: By medical decision making or total time on the date of the visit
By the number of history and exam elements documented
By the length of the note in words
By the number of diagnoses on the problem list
items.rationale: The 2021 changes set office E/M levels by medical decision making or total time, and history and exam only need to be medically appropriate. Counting elements was the old approach that encouraged bloat.

items.question: Which sequence best describes how an ambient AI scribe produces a note?
options: The clinician dictates the note and the software types it word for word
The patient completes a questionnaire that the AI converts into a signed note
The AI reads the chart and writes a note without listening to the visit
Consent, record the conversation, transcribe it, draft a note with a language model, then clinician review and signature
items.rationale: Ambient scribes capture the conversation with consent, convert speech to text, and use a generative model to draft new sentences, which the clinician must review and sign. Dictation records the clinician's own words; an ambient draft is composed by the model.

items.question: An AI draft states 'Patient reports a fall in the bathroom last week.' In the transcript, his wife reported the fall and the patient said he 'just slid down by the tub.' How should this error be classified?
options: Hallucination: the fall never happened
Omission: the fall is missing from the note
Wrong speaker: the report is attributed to the patient when his wife said it
Hedge removed: the note is more certain than the clinician was
items.rationale: The event was discussed, so it isn't invented or omitted. The error is attribution: the family member's report became the patient's, which also hides that the patient minimized it, a clinically useful fact.

items.question: Dr. Chen said, 'It could be the lisinopril, or low sugars overnight. I'm not sure yet.' The AI draft's assessment reads 'Orthostatic hypotension due to lisinopril.' What should she do before signing?
options: Sign it, since lisinopril is the most likely cause
Edit the assessment to restore the uncertainty and the plan to tell the two causes apart
Delete the assessment so the note has no diagnosis
Sign it now and add an amendment if the glucose log points elsewhere
items.rationale: The draft removed a hedge, turning an open question into a diagnosis that could anchor future care and steer attention away from hypoglycemia. Restoring the uncertainty keeps the note true. Signing and amending later lets the error spread first.

items.question: A vendor tells your CNO its ambient scribe will give every clinician 'an hour back each day.' Which response best reflects the 2025–2026 evidence?
options: Large studies show modest savings, about 16 documentation minutes per 8 scheduled hours, so pilot and measure locally
Agree: randomized trials show savings of about an hour per day
Decline: studies show ambient scribes increase documentation time
Agree, but only for nurses, because physician tools showed no benefit
items.rationale: The JAMA multisite study found about 16 fewer documentation minutes per 8 scheduled hours and no significant change in after-hours time, and a randomized trial found about 10% savings for one product and no significant difference for the other. Real but modest savings call for a local pilot with measurement.

items.question: Which statement best distinguishes a patient portal from a personal health record (PHR)?
options: A portal is a mobile app; a PHR is always on paper
A portal is only for scheduling; a PHR is only for results
A portal is run by the provider organization and tied to its EHR; a PHR is controlled by the patient
They are two names for the same thing
items.rationale: Houser distinguishes them by control: portals are provided by healthcare organizations and tied to their EHRs, while PHRs are managed by patients, who decide what goes in and who sees it. Both can be web or mobile, and portals do far more than scheduling.

items.question: A patient keeps a phone app where she types in her medications, allergies, and blood pressure readings. It isn't connected to any provider's system. What kind of record is this?
options: A tethered PHR
A standalone PHR
An integrated patient portal
A sponsored PHR
items.rationale: A standalone PHR is independent of any provider's EHR, with the patient entering and managing the data. Its main weakness is that accuracy depends on the patient keeping it current. Tethered and integrated types connect to provider systems; sponsored PHRs come from employers or insurers.

items.question: A clinic's EHR is set to hold every lab result from the portal for 72 hours so clinicians can review first. What is the main concern?
options: A blanket delay for all patients is likely information blocking under the Cures Act rules
The hold is too short; it should be one week
Holds are allowed as long as they're documented in the policy manual
Only the lab, not the clinic, can decide when results are released
items.rationale: Information blocking rules require that electronic health information not be withheld without a recognized exception. Exceptions are applied to specific situations, not as a blanket delay for everyone. A written policy doesn't turn a blanket hold into an exception.

items.question: Which situation most clearly supports delaying a patient's own access to a new result?
options: The result is abnormal and may upset the patient
The ordering clinician hasn't reviewed it yet
The result arrived after business hours
A licensed clinician documents that access is reasonably likely to endanger this specific patient's life or physical safety
items.rationale: The preventing-harm exception requires an individual determination of a real risk of harm, not general worry or convenience. Distress, pending review, and timing are the reasons blanket embargoes used to rely on, and none is enough by itself.

items.question: What did the OpenNotes study (Delbanco et al., 2012) find when patients were invited to read their doctors' notes?
options: Most patients were confused, and doctors stopped sharing notes
Patients read notes but reported no effect on their care
Most patients felt more in control, and few doctors reported more work
Message volume to doctors doubled
items.rationale: Across three sites, 77–87% of patients reported feeling more in control, many reported better medication adherence, only 1–8% reported worry or confusion, and doctors reported little change in workload. No participating doctor chose to stop.

items.question: Carmen Rivera, the mother of Mateo (14), asks the front desk to give her proxy full access to everything in his chart, including confidential visits. What should happen?
options: Grant full access because Mateo is a minor
Keep a limited proxy that excludes confidential adolescent care, as set by state law and policy, and let Mateo keep his own account
Deny all proxy access until Mateo turns 18
Give Carmen Mateo's password so she can see what he sees
items.rationale: Parents usually keep proxy access to routine information, but care a minor can consent to under state law stays confidential and is filtered from the proxy view. Full access ignores state law; no access ignores the parent's legitimate role; sharing a password removes both the limits and the audit trail.

items.question: Mateo Rivera turns 18. His mother still has proxy access to his portal. What should the system do?
options: End the parent's proxy automatically; any new access needs Mateo's own authorization
Keep the proxy in place until Mateo removes it
Convert the proxy to full access now that he's an adult
Keep the proxy until his mother's insurance no longer covers him
items.rationale: At the age of majority, a parent's authority to act for the patient ends, so proxy access should expire automatically. An adult can choose to give a family member access, but it must be his decision and documented. Insurance coverage doesn't create a right to see records.

items.question: Under the HIPAA Privacy Rule, does a provider need the patient's consent to share information with another provider for treatment?
options: Yes, always a signed consent form
Only when the information is shared electronically
Only if the patient is over 65
No; treatment, payment, and operations don't require consent under HIPAA, though stricter laws may
items.rationale: HIPAA permits use and disclosure for treatment, payment, and operations without consent, and requires an authorization for other purposes. Houser notes that some states and specific laws, such as Part 2, require more.

items.question: Marcus Reed is treated at Fordham's federally assisted addiction program. Primary care wants his treatment records. Under 42 CFR Part 2 as updated in 2024, what is required?
options: Nothing; HIPAA's treatment rule covers it
A court order
Marcus's written consent, which can be a single consent covering future treatment, payment, and operations
Approval from the addiction program's medical director only
items.rationale: Part 2 records need the patient's written consent to be shared. The 2024 rule, with compliance required by February 16, 2026, lets one consent cover future treatment, payment, and operations. HIPAA alone isn't enough, and a court order is needed only in specific circumstances.

items.question: Sofia Petrov, 78, tells the nurse her daughter Anna already uses her portal password to check her results. What is the best response?
options: Nothing; Sofia consented by sharing the password
Offer proxy access with Sofia's signed authorization, so Anna has her own login and a defined scope
Tell Sofia to change her password and stop Anna's access
Give Anna access to Sofia's chart in the clinician EHR instead
items.rationale: A shared password makes the audit trail show Sofia doing what Anna did and gives Anna unlimited access. Houser's best practices include never sharing login details. A proxy with Sofia's authorization keeps Anna's help and restores accountability.

items.question: At 4:50 p.m. Friday, a portal message says, "Chest pressure since last night, a little short of breath." It lands in a clinic pool with a 3-business-day auto-reply. What design change most directly prevents harm?
options: An urgent-word screen that sends an instant 'call 911' reply in the patient's language and moves the message to the top of the triage queue
Hire more nurses for the pool
Remind patients in the portal footer not to send urgent messages
Close the portal on weekends
items.rationale: Routing with an urgency screen acts in seconds, day or night. Staffing helps but doesn't change the order messages are read in. Footer reminders are widely ignored, and closing the portal removes access without fixing routing.

items.question: Fordham nurses forward about 9 of every 10 scheduling messages to the front desk. What routing change fits best?
options: Keep nurses reviewing them for hidden clinical issues
Have AI answer all scheduling messages with no human involved
Stop accepting scheduling requests through the portal
Send scheduling messages straight to the front desk at intake, with an urgent-word screen still applied
items.rationale: Routing by message type at intake takes non-clinical work off the nurse pool, and the urgent-word screen still catches the rare clinical message. Removing portal scheduling reduces access, and sending with no human in the loop has no one accountable.

items.question: Fordham's non-English portal messages wait a median of 71 hours for a reply, compared with 26 hours for English. Which fix best addresses the equity problem?
options: Ask non-English speakers to write in English
Put all non-English messages in a separate queue for the interpreter office
Route non-English messages by type like all others, reply in the patient's language with interpreter or certified bilingual support, and track reply time by language
Turn off portal messaging for patients who prefer another language
items.rationale: A separate language queue is what created the delay. Routing by type keeps urgent messages urgent in any language, and measuring by language shows whether the gap closes. The other options shift the burden to patients or remove access.

items.question: In the Stanford pilot of AI-drafted portal replies (Garcia et al., 2024), what happened?
options: Clinicians used most drafts and saved about a minute per message
Clinicians used about 20% of drafts, reported less burden and exhaustion, and saved no measurable time
The pilot was stopped after drafts harmed patients
Only physicians were allowed to use the drafts
items.rationale: Mean draft use was about 20%, task load and work exhaustion improved, and reading and reply times didn't change significantly. Nurses and pharmacists took part; GI nurses used drafts 29% of the time.

items.question: James O'Brien (type 2 diabetes, CKD 3a) writes that his sugar was 58 this morning and asks whether to take glipizide tonight. The AI draft says to continue it as prescribed. What should the nurse do?
options: Don't send it; check his medication changes and route to the prescriber today per the hypoglycemia protocol
Send the draft with a note that AI wrote it
Send the draft; it was generated from his chart
Tell him to stop all his diabetes medicines
items.rationale: A sulfonylurea after hypoglycemia, with reduced kidney function and a recent med change, needs clinical review. The nurse who sends a draft is accountable for it, and a disclosure doesn't make a wrong answer safe. Stopping every medicine is an unsafe overcorrection.

items.question: A health system reports that its patient-facing AI assistant cut billing messages by 58%. Leaders want to expand it to answer questions about lab results. What evidence matters most before expanding?
options: More reductions in billing messages
Patient satisfaction with the assistant's tone
The number of patients who opened the assistant
Accuracy and safe escalation on a clinician-reviewed sample of clinical questions
items.rationale: Fewer messages shows use, not correctness. Before an assistant answers clinical questions, clinicians should check its answers and confirm it escalates urgent problems to a human. Tone and usage don't show safety.

items.question: Fordham reports 64% portal activation overall and calls its portal a success. Which measure would best reveal a digital divide?
options: Total logins per month
The number of languages on the login page
Activation, messaging, and reply time broken out by preferred language, age, and disability
The portal's uptime percentage
items.rationale: Houser names the digital divide as a core challenge. An overall rate hides groups that fall out at each step. Stratified measures show where and for whom; uptime and available languages show availability, not use.

items.question: Which portal exchange could be billed as an e-visit (CPT 99421–99423)?
options: A refill request handled by protocol
A patient-started message about a new rash that takes an NP 12 minutes to evaluate, with no related visit in the past 7 days
A message asking to reschedule an appointment
A triage nurse's 5-minute call-back about a sore throat
items.rationale: E-visits are patient-initiated exchanges needing at least 5 minutes of a physician's or qualified health professional's evaluation over 7 days, not tied to a recent related visit. Refills, scheduling, and nurse-only triage don't qualify.

items.question: According to the NIST definition used in the textbook, usability is best described as:
options: How much users like a system when surveyed after go-live
How closely a screen follows the vendor's style guide
How few clicks a task requires in the vendor's demonstration
How well specific users reach their goals effectively, efficiently, and with satisfaction in a specific context
items.rationale: NIST defines usability as effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction for specified users in a specified context. Satisfaction alone, click counts in a demonstration, and visual consistency are each only a partial or indirect measure.

items.question: A nurse practitioner with three charts open places a potassium order on the wrong patient. Which design change most directly reduces this risk?
options: Add a pop-up reminding users to be careful
Require a longer password at login
Limit how many charts can be open at once and show the patient's name and photo at signing
Move the potassium order to a different order set
items.rationale: Wrong-patient orders happen when several charts are open and identity isn't prominent at the moment of signing. Limiting open charts and re-showing identity at signing targets that mechanism. Generic reminders are ignored, and passwords and order-set placement don't address identity.

items.question: Howe and colleagues found that about 0.03% of 1.7 million safety reports suggested EHR usability contributed to possible harm. What is the most accurate interpretation?
options: EHR usability rarely affects patient safety
The figure is a floor, because reporters usually describe the error rather than the screen design that caused it
Most usability problems occur in billing, not care
Safety reports overstate the role of technology
items.rationale: Safety reports are written by busy clinicians who describe what went wrong, not why the interface made it easy. The authors treat the count as an underestimate. The medication and ordering categories they found are clinical, not billing.

items.question: Which statement best distinguishes privacy from security under HIPAA?
options: Privacy sets the rules for who may use or disclose PHI and why; security protects electronic PHI's confidentiality, integrity, and availability
Privacy applies to paper records; security applies to electronic records only
Privacy is the patient's responsibility; security is the hospital's
They are two names for the same rule
items.rationale: The Privacy Rule governs permitted uses and disclosures of PHI in any form. The Security Rule sets administrative, physical, and technical safeguards for electronic PHI, organized around confidentiality, integrity, and availability.

items.question: Maria Diaz, the front desk lead, needs to schedule follow-up visits and verify insurance. Under minimum necessary, which access fits her role?
options: Full chart access, since she works in a covered entity
No access, since she isn't a clinician
Clinical notes only, so she can prioritize urgent patients
Schedule, demographics, and insurance, without clinical notes or results
items.rationale: Minimum necessary means access matched to the role's tasks. Scheduling and eligibility need demographics, the schedule, and coverage, not notes or results. No access would block legitimate work, and full access exceeds the need.

items.question: A nurse on 4 West learns that a friend from another unit was admitted to 6 North. The nurse can open the chart in the EHR. What should the nurse do?
options: Open the chart briefly to check that the friend is stable
Ask a 6 North nurse to read out the diagnosis
Not open the chart; visit or call the friend and let the friend decide what to share
Open the chart but avoid the notes section
items.rationale: Technical ability to open a chart is not permission to use it. With no treatment, payment, or operations purpose, any access, even brief or partial, or through a colleague, is an inappropriate use of PHI. The friend controls what to share.

items.question: A covering hospitalist must open a restricted chart for a patient in respiratory distress. What should a well-designed break-the-glass feature require?
options: A phone call to the privacy officer for approval before the chart opens
A stated reason at the moment of access, with the access logged and reviewed afterward
A permanent change to the hospitalist's role so this doesn't happen again
Nothing; restricted charts should open automatically in emergencies
items.rationale: Break-the-glass lets urgent care proceed without delay while keeping the default restrictive: the user states a reason, the access goes to a special audit trail, and it is reviewed. Waiting for approval delays care, and widening roles defeats minimum necessary.

items.question: An audit report shows a billing specialist opened a hospitalized coworker's notes and results at 00:12 from home, with no billing work-queue item for that account. What is the best next step for the analyst?
options: Refer the finding to the privacy officer with the log entries, for investigation under the sanction policy
Message the specialist and ask why they looked
Delete the entries so the coworker isn't upset
Take no action, because billing is a permitted purpose under HIPAA
items.rationale: The pattern (no work-queue item, clinical sections, off hours, a personal connection) suggests snooping. Payment is a permitted purpose only when there is real payment work. Investigation belongs to the privacy officer; confronting the user can compromise the investigation, and audit records must never be altered.

items.question: A dermatology clinic nurse used break-the-glass with the reason 'Emergency: immediate threat to life' on an inpatient's chart. The patient had no rapid response and no dermatology consult. How should the reviewer classify this access?
options: Appropriate, because break-the-glass was used correctly
Unknown until the patient files a complaint
Appropriate, because nurses may view any chart in the hospital
Not justified, because the stated reason doesn't match any evidence in the record
items.rationale: Break-the-glass records a claim; review checks it against evidence. With no emergency and no consult, the reason isn't supported, so the access is not justified and goes forward for investigation.

items.question: Which of the following is an administrative safeguard under the HIPAA Security Rule?
options: Automatic logoff on workstations
Locks on the data center door
A security risk analysis and a sanction policy
Encryption of laptops
items.rationale: Risk analysis, risk management, the sanction policy, and training are administrative safeguards. Automatic logoff and encryption are technical safeguards; facility locks are physical.

items.question: At 03:10 during a night shift, Jordan Park's phone shows a login approval prompt she didn't start. What should she do?
options: Approve it, since the prompt came from the hospital's real MFA app
Deny it and report it to the service desk right away
Ignore it; unanswered prompts expire on their own
Approve it and change her password in the morning
items.rationale: An unexpected MFA prompt means someone likely has her password. Denying blocks the login; reporting lets security reset credentials and look for other activity. Ignoring leaves the password compromised, and approving hands the attacker access.

items.question: Under the HIPAA Breach Notification Rule, a breach of unsecured PHI affecting 600 people in one state requires which notifications?
options: Notice to affected individuals within 60 days of discovery, to HHS at the same time, and to major media in that state
Notice to HHS only, in an annual report
Notice to the individuals only if they ask
No notice, if the organization believes no one was harmed
items.rationale: Breaches affecting 500 or more people require individual notice without unreasonable delay and within 60 days, contemporaneous notice to HHS (which posts it publicly), and media notice where 500 or more residents of a state are affected. Annual reporting applies only to breaches under 500.

items.question: The 2024 Change Healthcare attack halted claims and pharmacy eligibility checks at organizations that were never breached themselves. Which lesson for a hospital's risk analysis does this best support?
options: Only the EHR vendor needs to be in the risk analysis
Risk analysis should focus only on insider threats
Clearinghouses are exempt from HIPAA, so they carry no risk
Business associates and third-party services are part of the organization's risk, and downtime plans must cover their outages
items.rationale: Clearinghouses and other business associates handle PHI for covered entities and are bound by HIPAA. Their failure becomes the hospital's operational problem, so they belong in the risk analysis and in contingency planning.

items.question: At 02:14 the EHR on 4 West goes read-only. The 06:00 med pass includes insulin and a heparin drip adjustment. Which first actions show the best priorities?
options: Call the service desk every 15 minutes until the system is back
Hold all scheduled medications until the EHR returns
Declare downtime and assign roles, print the MAR and active orders from the downtime viewer, and start paper MARs with high-risk medications first
Document everything from memory once the system is restored
items.rationale: Safe downtime starts with a declared, organized response, current read-only information, and paper documentation that puts high-risk and time-critical medications first. Holding meds causes harm, repeated calls don't change the outage, and documenting from memory later is unreliable.

items.question: After a two-hour downtime, a nurse is back-entering a dose of piperacillin-tazobactam given on paper at 02:00. How should it be documented?
options: Entered with the current time, since that's when it's being charted
Entered with the original 02:00 administration time and marked as a late entry, then reconciled against the paper MAR
Left on paper only; the scanned paper MAR is enough
Entered as 'given' only if the patient remembers receiving it
items.rationale: Back-entry keeps the actual administration time so the next dose is timed correctly, marks the entry as late for transparency, and is reconciled against the paper source. Charting the current time invites a duplicate or mistimed dose, and paper-only records leave the EHR MAR showing the dose as overdue.

items.question: What are the SAFER Guides?
options: Free self-assessment checklists that help organizations evaluate EHR safety practices, including contingency planning
Federal regulations that fine hospitals for EHR outages
A vendor certification program for EHR usability
Nursing competency tests for downtime procedures
items.rationale: The SAFER (Safety Assurance Factors for EHR Resilience) Guides are self-assessment tools from the federal health IT office, covering areas such as contingency planning, patient identification, and system interfaces. They are not regulations, certifications, or competency tests.

items.question: After barcode medication administration goes live, the number of recorded medication errors on 4 West rises. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The barcode system is causing more errors than paper did
The data warehouse is double-counting events
Nurses are scanning less carefully than they charted on paper
The new system detects and records errors that paper processes missed, and may define late doses as errors
items.rationale: Houser notes that almost every barcode MAR go-live shows a rise in recorded errors because capture improves and the system's timing rules create new error states. Comparing before and after requires the same definitions, which is why baseline data matter.

items.question: Which pair of contingency-plan elements does the HIPAA Security Rule list as required, not addressable?
options: Cloud hosting and a second data center
Annual downtime drill and paper form inventory
Data backup plan and disaster recovery plan
Printer on backup power and a downtime PC on every unit
items.rationale: The contingency-plan standard requires a data backup plan, a disaster recovery plan, and an emergency mode operation plan; testing and criticality analysis are addressable. Drills, kits, and downtime PCs are good practice but aren't named as required specifications.

weeks.title: Clinical decision support and artificial intelligence

items.question: A pharmacist enters a new vancomycin order, and the system immediately runs a renal dosing check. In the CDS taxonomy, entering the order is the:
options: Trigger
Input data
Intervention
Offered choice
items.rationale: A trigger is the event that activates decision support, such as a new order. The creatinine and weight used by the check are input data; the dosing warning is the intervention; the suggested dose change is an offered choice.

items.question: What best distinguishes a predictive model from a generative AI tool in the EHR?
options: A predictive model works only on images; a generative tool works only on text
A predictive model uses rules written by clinicians; a generative tool learns from data
A predictive model is regulated by FDA; a generative tool never is
A predictive model estimates the probability of an event; a generative tool writes new content such as a note or summary
items.rationale: Houser contrasts discriminative models that classify or predict with generative AI that creates new text or images. Predictive models are learned from data, not hand-written rules, and regulation depends on intended use, not the model type.

items.question: During a 60-day silent pilot, 50 patients developed sepsis. The model alerted on 30 of them and on 170 patients who did not develop sepsis. What is the model's sensitivity?
items.rationale: Sensitivity is true positives divided by all patients with the condition: 30 ÷ 50 = 60%. Fifteen percent is the PPV (30 ÷ 200); 85% is roughly the specificity range; 30% confuses the count with a rate.

items.question: A sepsis model alerted on 200 patients on 4 West; 30 of them actually had sepsis. What is the positive predictive value, and what does it mean for the nurse?
options: 30%: the model catches 30% of sepsis cases
15%: roughly 1 in 7 alerted patients has sepsis
85%: most alerts will be real
60%: the model finds most septic patients
items.rationale: PPV is true positives divided by all alerts: 30 ÷ 200 = 15%. For the nurse, about six of every seven alerts will be false alarms, which predicts alert fatigue. Catching cases is sensitivity, a different number.

items.question: Specificity describes:
options: The share of patients without the condition whom the model correctly leaves unflagged
The share of alerts that turn out to be real cases
The share of real cases the model catches
How closely predicted risks match observed rates
items.rationale: Specificity is true negatives divided by all patients without the condition. The share of alerts that are real is PPV; the share of cases caught is sensitivity; agreement between predicted and observed risk is calibration.

items.question: A deterioration model fires 28 alerts a day on a unit with two 12-hour shifts and 7 RNs per shift. About how many alerts does each nurse receive per shift?
items.rationale: 28 alerts ÷ 2 shifts = 14 per shift; 14 ÷ 7 nurses = 2 per nurse per shift. Alerts per nurse per shift is a practical measure of burden and, combined with PPV, predicts alert fatigue.

items.question: A vendor reports that its deterioration model has an AUC of 0.88 at three academic hospitals. Your community hospital wants to turn it on next month. What is the best next step?
options: Ask the vendor for a higher AUC before deciding
Turn it on for all units, since an AUC of 0.88 is excellent
Run it silently on your own patients and measure PPV, sensitivity, and subgroup performance before anyone sees alerts
Turn it on and let nurses report problems through the help desk
items.rationale: Performance at other hospitals is a hypothesis. A silent local pilot shows how the model behaves on your patients, data, and workflows, including alert burden and subgroup gaps, before it changes care. Wong's study found a vendor-reported AUC of 0.76–0.83 dropped to 0.63 locally.

items.question: When Michigan Medicine independently validated the original Epic Sepsis Model (Wong et al., 2021), what did it find?
options: It matched the vendor's reported accuracy closely
It missed about two-thirds of sepsis cases while alerting on 18% of hospitalizations
It caught nearly every sepsis case but alerted on almost every patient
It performed well for adults but could not score older patients
items.rationale: Wong found an AUC of 0.63 versus the vendor's 0.76–0.83, sensitivity of 33% at the recommended threshold, PPV of 12%, and alerts on 18% of hospitalizations. Only 183 septic patients were flagged before clinicians had already started antibiotics.

items.question: Among 4 West patients a model labels '20–40% risk of deterioration', only 12% deteriorate. What is the best description of this problem?
options: The model is poorly calibrated: it overstates risk in that band
The model has low sensitivity
The model is biased against older adults
The model has high specificity
items.rationale: Calibration asks whether predicted risks match observed rates. A band labeled 20–40% in which 12% have the event overstates risk. The model might still rank patients well, but staff will learn to discount the number.

items.question: A sepsis model's PPV on 4 West fell from 22% to 9% over four months. During that time the lab changed lactate analyzers and a new triage protocol began. What is the most likely explanation, and what should happen?
options: The vendor updated the model. Accept the new performance
Nurses are documenting less. Retrain staff on flowsheet entry
Normal variation. No action is needed until a full year of data is available
Drift: the model's inputs changed. Report it to the model's owner and governance for investigation and recalibration
items.rationale: Changes in lab assays, workflows, or patient mix shift a model's inputs, which is drift. Monitoring exists to catch it; the owner and committee should investigate, recalibrate or retrain, and decide whether to pause the alert.

items.question: In a silent pilot, a sepsis model's sensitivity is 77% for patients who prefer English and 30% for patients who need an interpreter. What should the informatics team recommend?
options: Launch it only for English-speaking patients
Launch it, because overall sensitivity is acceptable
Do not launch as is; investigate why interpreter patients score lower (for example, missing documentation) and re-test before go-live
Ignore the gap, because subgroup numbers are always small
items.rationale: A large subgroup gap is a safety and equity problem even when overall numbers look acceptable. The team should find the cause, such as fewer documented assessments, fix it, and re-test. Deploying to only one language group would institutionalize the inequity; small numbers call for more data, not dismissal.

items.question: A Black patient with worsening shortness of breath has an SpO2 of 93% on the pulse oximeter. Given what is known about device bias, what is the best nursing action?
options: Document 93% and recheck in four hours, since it is within range
Assess the whole patient and escalate for arterial blood gas testing if the clinical picture suggests hypoxemia
Switch to a different pulse oximeter and accept the higher reading
Wait for the deterioration score to rise before escalating
items.rationale: Pulse oximeters have been shown to miss occult hypoxemia more often in Black patients. The nurse should not rely on one device value; clinical assessment and arterial blood gas testing guide escalation. Waiting for a score passes the device's bias into the model.

items.question: In the context of large language models, a 'hallucination' is:
options: Fluent content that is not supported by, or contradicts, the source information
A system crash that produces garbled text
A patient's report of symptoms captured in the transcript
A delay between the conversation and the draft appearing
items.rationale: A hallucination is plausible-sounding output that the source does not support, such as an invented lab value or an exam that was never performed. It is dangerous precisely because it reads like correct documentation.
