items.question: An AI-generated handoff summary for Sofia Petrov states 'no acute events overnight.' The flowsheet shows a fall at 02:15 and new confusion. What should the nurse do?
options: Add a comment to the flowsheet so the summary stays unchanged
Sign the summary, since the flowsheet is already available to the next nurse
Delete the summary and stop using the tool without telling anyone
Correct the summary against the source, hand off the fall and confusion, and report the error through the AI feedback process
items.rationale: The nurse who uses or signs AI output is accountable for it. The error must be corrected against the source, communicated at handoff, and reported so governance can track omissions. Silently abandoning the tool hides the failure from the people who can fix it.

items.question: Bedi and colleagues (2025) reviewed 519 studies of large language models in health care. Which finding most limits the use of those studies to justify an AI handoff tool on a nursing unit?
options: Most studies focused on nursing documentation
Most studies found LLMs less accurate than chance
Only about 5% used real patient care data, and few assessed bias or deployment
The studies were all conducted outside the United States
items.rationale: Most studies tested knowledge questions rather than real patient data, and very few measured fairness, calibration, or deployment. Evidence from exam-style benchmarks does not show how a tool will perform on real nursing handoffs.

items.question: ONC's HTI-1 'decision support intervention' requirements, in effect since January 2025, mainly require certified EHR developers to:
options: Obtain FDA clearance for every predictive model
Make 'source attributes' about predictive tools available to users, such as intended use, development data, and fairness testing
Guarantee a minimum PPV of 20% for all alerts
Let patients opt out of all predictive models
items.rationale: HTI-1 requires transparency: users can see source attributes describing a predictive tool, similar to a model card. It does not set accuracy thresholds or require FDA clearance, and a 2025 proposal (HTI-5) would remove these requirements.

items.question: Under FDA's approach to clinical decision support software, which tool is most likely to be treated as a regulated medical device?
options: A time-critical sepsis alarm that tells nurses to act but does not show the basis for its recommendation
An order set that lists the hospital's sepsis bundle
A drug reference the nurse can look up
A rule that displays a guideline link when a diagnosis is entered
items.rationale: FDA's guidance turns largely on whether a clinician can independently review the basis of a recommendation. A 'black box' alarm directing time-critical action is the most device-like. Order sets, references, and guideline links let clinicians see and judge the content.

items.question: Fordham Health wants to turn on a vendor deterioration model for all medical-surgical units. Which plan reflects sound AI governance?
options: The vendor monitors the model and reports problems when it finds them
The CIO approves it because it came with the EHR upgrade
Each unit manager decides independently whether to use it
A multidisciplinary AI committee, including bedside nursing, reviews local validation, approves a threshold and workflow, names an owner, and sets a monitoring schedule and stop rule
items.rationale: Governance means evidence, ownership, and ongoing oversight: local validation, a deliberate threshold and workflow, a named owner, subgroup monitoring, and a stop rule decided before launch, with nursing at the table. Vendor-only monitoring or unit-by-unit decisions leave no one accountable.

items.question: Which level of interoperability means two systems exchange data and interpret it the same way because they use shared codes?
options: Foundational
Semantic
Structural
Organizational
items.rationale: Semantic interoperability depends on standard vocabularies such as LOINC, SNOMED CT, and RxNorm so the receiver understands the data as the sender meant it. Foundational is arrival only, structural preserves format and field placement, and organizational covers policy and workflow.

items.question: A skilled nursing facility receives Sofia Petrov's discharge summary as a scanned PDF attached to a secure message. Nurses can read it, but nothing imports into the medication list. What is the highest level of interoperability achieved?
options: Foundational
Structural
Semantic
Organizational
items.rationale: The data arrived and a human can read it, which is foundational. Because nothing lands in structured fields, structural and semantic interoperability were not achieved, and organizational interoperability requires the lower levels plus policy and workflow.

items.question: A SNF receives a fully coded discharge document that imports correctly, but no one is assigned to review incoming documents, and it sits unread for two days. At which level did the exchange fail?
options: Foundational, because the document was delayed
Structural, because the fields did not display
Semantic, because the codes were not understood
Organizational, because no policy or person acted on it
items.rationale: Delivery, structure, and meaning all worked. The failure was in workflow and accountability, which is organizational interoperability. Blaming the technical levels leads to the wrong fix.

items.question: Which description best fits HL7 version 2?
options: A web-based standard that sends one resource at a time as JSON
An XML clinical document such as a discharge summary
Event messages with fields separated by pipe characters, used mostly inside hospitals for admissions, orders, and results
A federal list of data elements every EHR must exchange
items.rationale: HL7 v2 messages are terse, event-driven, and pipe-delimited, and they still carry most in-hospital traffic. JSON resources describe FHIR, XML documents describe CDA and C-CDA, and the federal data list is USCDI.

items.question: Before a visit, an outside cardiologist's EHR requests only Sofia's current allergies and active medications from Fordham, item by item, over the web. Which standard fits this request best?
options: An HL7 v2 admission (ADT) message
A FHIR API returning AllergyIntolerance and MedicationRequest resources
A C-CDA continuity of care document
A faxed medication list
items.rationale: FHIR APIs let a system request specific resources rather than a whole document. A C-CDA would send an entire summary, HL7 v2 ADT messages carry admission events inside a hospital, and a fax cannot be computed on.

items.question: A nurse manager wants a fall-risk app that runs inside the EHR and could be reused at hospitals on different vendors. What makes that possible?
options: SMART on FHIR: a standard app launch and permission step on top of FHIR data
A custom HL7 v2 interface built for each hospital
Exporting a C-CDA document each shift
Screen scraping the EHR's display
items.rationale: SMART on FHIR standardizes how an app launches inside the EHR, gets permission, and reads FHIR data, so one app can run in any conforming EHR. Custom interfaces and exports must be rebuilt per site, and screen scraping is fragile and unsafe.

items.question: Which vocabulary is the standard for naming a clinical drug such as 'apixaban 5 mg oral tablet'?
options: LOINC
SNOMED CT
ICD-10-CM
RxNorm
items.rationale: RxNorm provides normalized names and codes for clinical drugs and links brand and generic names. LOINC names tests and observations, ICD-10-CM classifies diagnoses, and SNOMED CT covers clinical findings and concepts.

items.question: Maple Grove's lab reports potassium under the local code 'K+ SER.' In the cardiologist's EHR, those results appear as a different test from Fordham's potassium and won't trend together. What fixes this?
options: Ask Maple Grove to fax results instead
Code the result with ICD-10-CM
Map both local codes to the same LOINC code for serum potassium
Rename the test 'Potassium' in the display
items.rationale: LOINC gives tests a shared identifier so results from different labs are recognized as the same observation. A display rename changes only the label, ICD-10-CM codes diagnoses rather than tests, and faxing removes structure altogether.

items.question: Sofia's sulfa allergy was typed as a free-text comment at Fordham. Her discharge summary reached Maple Grove, yet no alert fired when a sulfonamide antibiotic was ordered. What is the best explanation?
options: Maple Grove uses a different EHR vendor, so it cannot read Fordham's data
No coded allergen was sent, so the receiving system had nothing to match against the order
HIPAA blocked the allergy from being shared without consent
FHIR does not support allergy data
items.rationale: Decision support matches coded data. A free-text comment travels as words, not as a coded allergen, so the receiving system could not trigger a drug-allergy check. Different vendors exchange coded data routinely, HIPAA permits sharing for treatment, and FHIR has an AllergyIntolerance resource.

items.question: What is USCDI?
options: A standardized set of health data classes and elements that certified EHRs must be able to exchange
A national patient identifier used to match records
The network of QHINs created by TEFCA
A billing code set for outpatient procedures
items.rationale: USCDI defines which data, such as allergies, medications, problems, results, and preferred language, must be exchangeable. It is not an identifier, a network, or a billing code set.

items.question: At discharge, Fordham automatically sends Sofia's discharge summary to Maple Grove's secure Direct address. What type of exchange is this?
options: Query-based exchange
Public health reporting
Consumer-mediated exchange
Directed exchange
items.rationale: Directed exchange pushes information to a known recipient, commonly with the Direct protocol. Query-based exchange pulls records on request, and consumer-mediated exchange is gathered and shared by the patient.

items.question: A SNF nurse calls for a patient's recent echocardiogram report to guide treatment. No signed release is on file. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Refuse until the patient signs an authorization
Send it only if both organizations use the same EHR vendor
Send it: HIPAA permits disclosure to another provider for treatment, and unnecessary delay may be information blocking
Tell the SNF to ask the patient to request it through the portal
items.rationale: HIPAA permits disclosures for treatment without authorization, and the Cures Act prohibits practices likely to interfere with exchange unless an exception applies. Requiring a release or routing through the patient delays care without a legal basis.

items.question: Under TEFCA, what is a QHIN?
options: A hospital's internal interface engine
A qualified health information network that has signed the Common Agreement and exchanges with other QHINs
A federal registry of patient consents
An app store for SMART on FHIR apps
items.rationale: QHINs are networks designated under TEFCA that connect to each other under one Common Agreement, so participants on one QHIN can reach participants on others. The other options describe different components.

items.question: An outside AllergyIntolerance says 'penicillin: rash, severity not recorded' with a 98% identity match. Fordham's chart says 'penicillin: hives, severe.' What is the best reconciliation decision?
options: Keep the local entry and record the outside reaction with its source in the reason
Accept the incoming item and replace the local entry because it is newer
Defer until the outside clinic sends a severity
Remove the allergy because the sources disagree
items.rationale: With confident identity and conflicting content, keep the more specific and safer local value and preserve the outside reaction with provenance. Replacing it lowers safety, deferring leaves a confident item unresolved, and deleting an allergy because of disagreement is dangerous.

items.question: A Condition resource for 'atrial fibrillation' arrives for 'Sofiya Petrova' with a 71% identity match; the birth year differs by one digit. The story fits Sofia's history. What should happen first?
options: Accept it, because the diagnosis matches her history
Merge it into her problem list as a historical problem
Reject it permanently because the name is spelled differently
Defer it for identity review and make no clinical decision until the match is resolved
items.rationale: Every clinical judgment assumes the item belongs to this patient. At low confidence, defer to identity review; the fitting clinical story is the trap. Rejecting permanently could discard genuine history once identity is confirmed.

items.question: At SNF admission, Sofia's pre-admission list (from her primary care clinic, March) shows metoprolol tartrate 25 mg twice daily. Fordham's discharge list (Tuesday) shows metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily. What is the best reconciliation?
options: Continue both, since they came from two trusted sources
Use the clinic list, since the primary care clinician knows her best
Use the discharge list as current, mark the tartrate order stopped, and confirm with the patient or daughter and the pharmacist
Hold both until the cardiologist visit in three weeks
items.rationale: Provenance decides: the discharge list is the most recent and reflects an intentional change during the admission. Continuing both is a duplication error, preferring the older source ignores when each fact was true, and holding a beta-blocker in heart failure for weeks creates harm.

items.question: In CMS122, the eCQM for diabetes A1c poor control (above 9%), how is a patient with no A1c during the measurement period counted?
options: Excluded from the denominator
Counted in the numerator as poorly controlled
Counted as controlled
Reported separately and not counted
items.rationale: CMS122 is an inverse measure that places patients with no A1c in the numerator, treating missing testing as poor control. This is why definitions matter: the same missing data would be excluded or ignored under other rules.

items.question: A clinic's registry has 40 patients with diabetes. Thirty have a final A1c this year, and 6 of those are above 9%. A manager's slide says '15% of our diabetics are uncontrolled.' What is the main problem?
options: It divides by all 40 without stating that 10 patients have no result, so it treats untested patients as controlled
The math is wrong; 6 of 40 is 20%
Registries shouldn't be used for quality reporting
A1c isn't a valid measure of diabetes control
items.rationale: Six of 40 is 15%, but that denominator quietly counts ten untested patients as controlled. The report should state the definition, use the evaluable denominator (6 of 30, 20%) or a stated rule for missing data, and report the ten missing.

items.question: What is the main difference between a request for information (RFI) and a request for proposal (RFP)?
options: An RFI requests pricing only; an RFP requests references only
An RFI is sent only after contract signing; an RFP is sent before
An RFI asks broad questions to narrow a large field; an RFP asks a short list of vendors to respond to the organization's detailed requirements
An RFI is legally binding on the vendor; an RFP is not
items.rationale: Houser describes the RFI as a broad first screen sent to perhaps 10 to 20 vendors to reach a manageable short list, and the RFP as a structured document sent to four or five vendors asking them to respond to the organization's functional requirements with comparable answers.

items.question: A functional needs assessment is best described as:
options: A list of features copied from the leading vendor's brochure
A statement of the capabilities the organization needs to meet its goals, drawn from workflow analysis, user input, and gaps in current systems
A comparison of vendor prices after demonstrations
The vendor's test plan for go-live
items.rationale: The functional needs assessment outlines the capabilities required to realize the organization's EHR goals and relies on workflow and process mapping, user surveys, interviews, and gap analysis. It is written vendor-neutral, before products are compared.

items.question: After a flawless vendor-led demonstration, a committee member wants to select the vendor immediately. What is the strongest next step?
options: Have every finalist run the same scripted scenarios from the needs assessment, scored by frontline users, then check references at similar sites
Ask the vendor for a second, longer demonstration of its best features
Select the vendor; a good demo is strong evidence of fit
Ask the salesperson for written assurance that nurses will like it
items.rationale: Vendor-led demos show products at their best. Scripted scenarios run identically for every vendor and scored by users produce comparable evidence; site visits and references at similar organizations test real-world use. A salesperson's assurance is not evidence.

items.question: Using weighted scoring, Vendor X rates 4 on usability (weight 3) and 2 on cost (weight 5). Vendor Y rates 2 on usability and 4 on cost. On these two criteria, which is true?
options: X leads, 22 to 20
They tie at 22
X leads, because usability matters most to nurses
Y leads, 26 to 22
items.rationale: Multiply each rating by its weight and add. X: 4×3 + 2×5 = 12 + 10 = 22. Y: 2×3 + 4×5 = 6 + 20 = 26. The weights, set before scoring, decide which strengths count most.

items.question: A vendor's RFP response promised one on-site trainer for every four nurses at go-live. The signed contract doesn't mention go-live support. What is the most accurate statement?
options: The promise is enforceable because it was in writing
The promise is enforceable only if the vendor is publicly traded
The promise may not be enforceable; RFP responses and implementation plans should be incorporated into the contract
Go-live support is always included in EHR licenses by regulation
items.rationale: Houser notes that the vendor's RFP response and implementation plan are not legally binding by themselves; they must be made part of the contract so expectations are clear and enforceable.

items.question: A hosting contract guarantees 99.9% uptime. About how much unplanned downtime does that still allow per year?
options: About 9 minutes
About 9 hours
About 3.6 days
None; 99.9% means continuous availability
items.rationale: A year has 8,760 hours. 0.1% of 8,760 is about 8.8 hours. Uptime and reliability belong in vendor comparisons and contracts, along with how planned downtime is counted and what happens when the target is missed.

items.question: A 90-bed hospital joins a large health system's Epic through Community Connect. Its nurses want to redesign the admission flowsheet extensively for their unit. What is the most likely constraint?
options: Local customization is limited; changes usually go through the host's standard build and governance
None; Community Connect sites build their own instance
The hospital must buy its own servers first
Flowsheets cannot be used in hosted systems
items.rationale: In Community Connect the affiliate joins the host's instance, which the host configures and upgrades. In exchange for lower cost and a shared record, local customization and control of the upgrade calendar are limited, similar to the 'borrow' acquisition models Houser describes.

items.question: In Houser's terms, a 'big bang' rollout means:
options: Converting all paper charts before choosing a vendor
Running the old and new systems side by side for several months
Implementing one module in one unit as a pilot
Implementing all parts of the system across all units at virtually the same time
items.rationale: A big bang (rapid) implementation brings the whole system, or a whole component, live across the organization at once. Running systems side by side is parallel processing; a single-unit start is a pilot or phased approach.

items.question: A single-site, single-specialty practice with 12 providers is replacing its EHR, with strong vendor support available. Which rollout is best supported by the textbook's guidance?
options: Phased by provider over 18 months
Parallel processing on paper and electronic for a year
Big bang: everyone switches together
A pilot with one provider, then a decision in two years
items.rationale: Houser's rollout table suggests big bang for single-specialty or small clinics, especially with good support. A long phased rollout would create a costly hybrid record in a small practice where everyone shares patients.

items.question: During a barcode medication administration go-live, a hospital requires nurses to document on both paper MARs and the eMAR for a month. What problem does the textbook warn about?
options: Parallel processing is illegal under HIPAA
Parallel processing is labor-intensive and error-prone, and inconsistent use of the two can be mistaken for system flaws
Parallel processing prevents the vendor from providing support
There is no downside; it is the safest approach for any system
items.rationale: Houser describes a hospital where some nurses mainly used the barcode MAR and others the paper form; the oversight team mistook the inconsistency for system flaws. Parallel processing doubles work and invites errors, so it is used selectively.

items.question: Nurses understand why barcode scanning prevents errors, support it, and completed training. On go-live night they cannot scan because the wristbands don't read. In ADKAR terms, which element failed?
options: Ability
Desire
Knowledge
Awareness
items.rationale: Awareness, desire, and knowledge are in place. Ability, being able to perform the change in real work, failed because of equipment. More training won't fix an ability barrier; working devices and at-the-elbow support will.

items.question: A test follows a heparin order from the prescriber to pharmacy verification, label printing, bedside scanning, and MAR documentation. What kind of testing is this?
options: Unit testing
Acceptance testing 60 days after go-live
Usability testing of one screen
Integrated testing
items.rationale: Integrated testing follows a complete workflow across systems and handoffs. Unit testing checks a single piece of build; acceptance in EHR contracts is often declared 30 to 60 days after go-live.

items.question: A mock data conversion of 24,000 patient records reports 98.7% required-field completeness. The signed threshold is 99.5%. What is the best interpretation?
options: The load passes; 98.7% rounds to 99%
Conversion quality doesn't matter because nurses will re-enter data at the first visit
About 312 charts have missing required data; the threshold isn't met, so failures should be sampled, mappings fixed, and another trial load run
The threshold should be lowered to 98.5% so go-live can proceed
items.rationale: 1.3% of 24,000 is about 312 charts, each potentially missing an allergy, medication, or problem. The agreed threshold was not met. The right response is to sample failures against source records, fix the mapping, and repeat the trial load, not to move the threshold.

items.question: A project budget assumes super-users will train all 400 nurses during their regular shifts, with no backfill funding. What is the main risk?
options: Super-users will know too much about the system
Training costs are underestimated; super-users carrying full assignments can't train or support peers well, so training quality and go-live support suffer
The vendor will refuse to provide software
Nurses will be trained too early
items.rationale: Houser warns that overreliance on superuser training models leads to underestimated training budgets and that early users become overburdened as informal trainers. Protected time and backfill belong in the budget.

items.question: In the context of EHR implementation, when is acceptance testing (the organization affirming the system works as intended) usually completed?
options: Often 30 to 60 days or more after go-live
During unit testing of individual screens
Before the vendor is selected
On the day the contract is signed
items.rationale: Houser notes that for EHRs, acceptance generally comes 30 to 60 days after go-live or longer, because not every scenario can be predicted before the system runs in real operations.

items.question: One week after go-live, a nurse whom managers expected to struggle has filed no tickets and hasn't asked for help. What should the support team conclude?
options: The nurse has mastered the system
Nothing; only reported problems need attention
Remove the nurse's super-user support to save staff
Check usage: the nurse may not be using the system or may be using workarounds
items.rationale: Houser advises checking in with all users, not only those who report problems: someone expected to struggle who shows no difficulty may not be using the system. Simple usage reports can confirm whether documentation is being done as intended.

items.question: Ball and colleagues (2024) found that at the VA's first Oracle Cerner site, upbeat official messages that downplayed problems made things worse. Which change management principle does this most directly support?
options: Communication should stop after go-live to avoid alarm
Only executives should communicate about the EHR
Communication should be honest and continue after implementation, acknowledging challenges and course corrections
Staff should be told problems are temporary regardless of evidence
items.rationale: Houser's discussion of change communication stresses plain, targeted messages and continued communication after implementation about successes, challenges, and course corrections. Messaging that denies what staff experience erodes trust and slows adoption.

items.question: In a RACI chart for a go-live, several people are marked 'A' (accountable) for the go/no-go decision. Why is this a problem?
options: It isn't; more accountability is always better
Each person may assume another will decide, so the decision can fall through; each task should have exactly one accountable owner
RACI charts do not allow executives to be listed
Only the vendor can be accountable for go-live
items.rationale: RACI assigns responsible, accountable, consulted, and informed roles. One accountable owner per task makes decision rights clear, which Houser's discussion of steering committees, project managers, and sponsors emphasizes.

weeks.title: Optimization, measurement, and AI project clinic

items.question: According to Houser, what is EHR optimization?
options: Replacing the EHR with a newer vendor's product
Installing the vendor's scheduled software upgrades
The initial build and configuration completed before go-live
Fine-tuning a live EHR to meet users' needs and improve productivity and efficiency
items.rationale: Houser defines optimization as fine-tuning an EHR to fit the practice and improve clinical productivity and efficiency, using user feedback, training, and fixes. Initial build happens before go-live, upgrades are maintenance, and replacing the vendor is a new implementation.

items.question: A clinic complains that refilling a routine prescription takes 14 clicks and that nobody was trained on shortcuts. Which approach best reflects an optimization sprint?
options: Add the request to the vendor's next annual upgrade list
Assign an online training module to every clinic user
Send a small team of trainers and analysts on-site for about two weeks to fix build issues and teach personalization
Ask the clinic manager to remind staff to work faster
items.rationale: Sieja's sprints put a small team of trainers, analysts, and clinician builders in one clinic for about two weeks to fix local build problems, teach personalization, and redesign workflow. An annual upgrade list is slow, generic modules miss the local problem, and reminders put the burden on people.

items.question: In EHR usage reports, what does 'pajama time' measure?
options: Time spent documenting on night shift
EHR activity outside scheduled working hours
Time a patient spends waiting for discharge after midnight
Minutes a workstation stays logged in while idle
items.rationale: Pajama time is EHR work done outside scheduled hours; Epic's definition counts activity outside 7 a.m.–5:30 p.m. on weekdays. For shift nurses the equivalent is after-shift charting. It is not night-shift work, patient wait time, or idle log-in time.

items.question: Audit logs show 4 West nurses average 86 minutes per shift in flowsheets, far more than a similar unit. What can the log data NOT tell you on its own?
options: Why nurses spend that time, such as redundancy, acuity, or interruptions
How flowsheet time changed month to month
Which flowsheet sections take the most time
Which shifts have the highest flowsheet time
items.rationale: Logs record what was done, when, and for how long, so they can break time down by section, month, and shift. They cannot explain why: redundant rows, sicker patients, or interruptions. That requires observation, interviews, or a survey, as Cho and colleagues did.

items.question: After a flowsheet redesign, time in flowsheets drops 12 minutes per shift, but completed fall-risk reassessments drop from 94% to 81%. What does this pattern suggest?
options: The redesign succeeded because the primary measure improved
The audit log is wrong because both numbers should move together
Fall-risk reassessments are a process measure, so the drop doesn't matter
The balancing measure shows a possible harm; check whether the redesign hid or removed the reassessment row
items.rationale: The fall-risk reassessment rate is acting as a balancing measure, and it flags a possible harm: the time saved may have come from documentation that disappeared. Declaring success ignores that harm, process measures still matter for safety, and there is no reason the two numbers must move together.

items.question: Which of the following is an outcome measure rather than a process measure?
options: Percent of shifts with a documented fall-risk reassessment
Percent of nurses who completed flowsheet training
Inpatient falls with injury per 1,000 patient days
Percent of patients with a bed alarm order
items.rationale: Outcome measures track changes in patients' health status, such as falls with injury. The others count whether steps of care happened, which makes them process measures. Houser notes that better processes don't automatically produce better outcomes, so both are needed.

items.question: An ambient AI nursing documentation pilot aims to reduce after-shift charting. Which is the best balancing measure?
options: After-shift charting minutes per nurse
Minutes nurses spend reviewing and correcting AI drafts, and errors found in signed notes
Number of nurses enrolled in the pilot
The vendor's reported time savings
items.rationale: A balancing measure watches for harm or extra work the change might create elsewhere; draft correction time and errors in signed notes do that. After-shift minutes are the primary outcome, enrollment is an adoption count, and the vendor's figure is a claim, not a local measure.

items.question: Which goal best meets the SMART criteria?
options: Reduce average after-shift charting on 4 West from 38 to 25 minutes per nurse by March 31, measured weekly from audit logs
Make flowsheets easier for nurses as soon as possible
Reduce documentation burden on 4 West
Cut all nursing documentation time in half this year
items.rationale: The SMART goal names the unit, the metric, the baseline, the target, the deadline, and the data source. The others are vague, have no measure or date, or set an unrealistic target that ignores what documentation is required.

items.question: Why does Houser say a benefits realization study needs a baseline collected before the change?
options: Vendors require baseline data before they sign a contract
A baseline guarantees the project will show a positive ROI
Baselines replace the need for measuring after go-live
Without a baseline, comparisons after implementation rely on guesswork and opinion
items.rationale: Houser notes that a benefits realization study done without baseline values relies heavily on guesswork and on subjective satisfaction or dissatisfaction. A baseline doesn't replace later measurement, isn't a vendor contract requirement, and can't guarantee a positive result.

items.question: A nursing informatics team wants to replace three duplicate pain rows with one source row. Following PDSA, what should happen first after planning?
options: Build the change for all units at once so everyone benefits
Survey nurses about the idea and skip the test if most agree
Test it with a small group of nurses on one unit for about two weeks and study the data against baseline
Wait for the vendor to deliver a standard pain flowsheet
items.rationale: PDSA tests a change on a small scale first, then studies the results, including balancing measures, before adopting, adapting, or abandoning it. Hospital-wide build skips the test, a survey measures opinion rather than effect, and waiting on the vendor isn't a test at all.

items.question: After barcode medication administration goes live, the reported medication error rate rises from 5% to 10%. What is the best first interpretation?
options: The barcode system is causing more medication errors
Measurement became more precise; errors that paper missed are now being detected
Nurses are scanning incorrectly and need discipline
The go-live should be rolled back immediately
items.rationale: Houser's BC-MAR case shows that a more precise system can raise reported error rates because it captures errors that paper documentation missed. The right move is to investigate before concluding safety got worse; blaming nurses or rolling back ignores the measurement change.

items.question: A study finds that heavy users of an ambient AI scribe spent 21% less time in notes than light users. Why can't you conclude the tool caused the whole difference?
options: Heavy users chose to use the tool heavily and may differ from light users in other ways
Audit-log data can never measure time in notes
The difference is too small to matter clinically
Ambient AI tools only affect physicians, not note time
items.rationale: Clinicians who adopt a tool heavily are self-selected and may already be faster, more comfortable with technology, or have different patients. That is a comparison of groups, not a controlled test. Log data does measure note time, and a 21% difference is not trivial.

items.question: A vendor tells your CNO that its AI tool cut documentation time by 42% at another health system. What is the best response?
options: Buy it, because the result came from a real customer
Reject it, because vendor numbers are always false
Ask the other health system's CNO whether she likes it
Treat the figure as a hypothesis and plan a local pilot with a baseline, a comparison unit, and balancing measures
items.rationale: Vendor-cited results come from another setting and are chosen by the vendor, so they are claims to test, not proof. A local pilot with a baseline, a comparison, and balancing measures gives evidence for your units. Automatic rejection and a single testimonial are both weak evidence.

items.question: A large study found ambient scribe adopters generated about $3,044 more per physician per year, with modest volume gains. Your hospital pays more than that per license. Which justification for keeping the tool is strongest?
options: Revenue will eventually exceed the license cost
The tool is popular, so cost doesn't matter
Measured reductions in burnout, turnover, and after-hours work, weighed against cost with a baseline
Competitors use ambient AI, so we must too
items.rationale: When direct revenue does not cover cost, the case rests on outcomes such as burnout, retention, and after-hours time, measured against a baseline and valued honestly (turnover has a real cost). Hoping revenue grows, popularity, and keeping up with competitors are not evidence.

items.question: An AI shift summary is accurate overall, but summaries for patients who need an interpreter need edits twice as often. What should the analyst do?
options: Report the overall accuracy, since the average meets the target
Stratify results by language, report the gap, and restrict or add review for those patients until it is fixed
Stop using interpreters so the tool works better
Ignore it, because interpreter patients are a small group
items.rationale: Checking results across patient groups is how you find algorithmic bias; an average can hide a subgroup where the tool fails. The fix is to report the gap and add safeguards for that group. Reporting only the average, dropping interpreters, or dismissing a small group all harm the patients most at risk.

items.question: In a financial impact analysis, what does the payback period measure?
options: The time needed to recover the initial investment from the project's gains
The interest rate at which net present value equals zero
The total cost of ownership over five years
The difference between projected and actual benefits
items.rationale: The payback period is the time it takes to recoup the initial investment. The interest rate at which NPV is zero is the internal rate of return; total cost of ownership sums all costs; comparing projected and actual benefits is a benefits realization study.

items.question: A project team demonstrates its AI discharge summary tool on three polished cases and says it is faster than the current template. What is missing for a baseline comparison?
options: More polished cases so the speed difference is convincing
The accuracy figure a vendor published for a similar tool
A survey asking nurses whether they prefer the tool
The same cases run through the current workflow with the same scoring sheet
items.rationale: A baseline is the current workflow measured on the same cases with the same scoring, so any difference can be attributed to the tool. More polished cases make a longer demonstration, not a comparison; a preference survey measures opinion; a vendor's figure comes from different cases and scoring.

items.question: A team is writing the rollback trigger for a limited pilot of its AI draft tool. Which is a true rollback trigger?
options: A monthly meeting at which the pilot's progress is discussed
The sponsor's judgment at the end of the pilot
Any signed note found to contain an invented order, or more than two corrections per draft for a week
Users saying the tool feels slower than the template
items.rationale: A rollback trigger is an observable event with a threshold that stops the release without waiting for a meeting. A review meeting and a sponsor's judgment are governance steps, and a feeling of slowness has no measure or owner. Continuous monitoring is how AI stays safe after go-live.

items.question: In Singh and Sittig's Health IT Safety Framework, which activity belongs to the domain 'using health IT to monitor and improve safety'?
options: Reviewing audit-log data each week to find AI drafts signed without edits
Training nurses to scan the patient's wristband rather than a copy
Testing that an interface maps a critical lab flag correctly before go-live
Choosing a vendor whose EHR is certified by ONC
items.rationale: Using audit logs and dashboards to find safety problems is the third domain: health IT as a monitoring tool. Interface testing belongs to making the technology itself safe, wristband training belongs to using it safely, and certification is a purchasing requirement rather than a safety-monitoring activity.

items.question: Nurses on a unit scan barcodes taped to the medication cart because the scanner cord does not reach the bed. The scanner and eMAR work correctly. Which safety domain is failing?
options: Safe health IT: the technology is defective
None: this is a staffing problem, not a health IT problem
Using health IT to improve safety: the monitoring is missing
Using health IT safely: the system works but is not used as intended
items.rationale: The technology works as designed, but the way it is used defeats its purpose, which is the 'use it safely' domain. Physical layout and workflow drive the workaround, so the fix involves the environment and process, not the software. Calling it only a staffing problem ignores the equipment and workflow causes.

items.question: Over two months, the share of AI-drafted nursing notes edited before signing falls from 32% to 23%, median time to sign falls to 11 seconds, and chart audits find more omissions. What is the most likely interpretation?
options: The AI model has improved, so fewer edits are needed
Nurses have become more efficient with training
Review is turning into automatic approval
The audit sample is too small to mean anything
items.rationale: Fewer edits alone could mean a better model, but fewer edits, faster signing, and rising omissions together point to review becoming a rubber stamp. Training would not explain the rise in omissions. The audit finding is the harm-based measure that separates the two explanations, so it should not be dismissed without evidence.

items.question: Which of these is NOT one of the eight dimensions of Sittig and Singh's sociotechnical model?
options: Workflow and communication
Vendor market share
External rules, regulations, and pressures
System measurement and monitoring
items.rationale: The eight dimensions are hardware and software, clinical content, the human-computer interface, people, workflow and communication, internal organizational policies, external rules and pressures, and measurement and monitoring. Market share can influence decisions but is not a dimension of the model.

items.question: An AI agent will queue potassium replacement orders for 4 West patients on the electrolyte protocol. Which design keeps human oversight meaningful?
options: The agent queues the order; the nurse reviews the value, renal function, and patient before releasing it, and the agent stops and pages when data are unclear
The agent places and releases orders itself, and a report goes to the nurse manager weekly
Every queued order generates an interruptive alert that the nurse must click through
The agent runs only on night shift, when staffing is lowest and help is most needed
items.rationale: Meaningful oversight means a person reviews the specific facts before the action and the agent defers to a human when it is uncertain. A weekly report comes after harm is possible. Click-through alerts create alert fatigue rather than review. Running only at night puts the least-supervised tool where oversight is thinnest.

items.question: Devices and ambient AI chart a patient's overnight vital signs. What should the nurse's attestation step require?
options: One signature for the whole shift, to save time
A second nurse to co-sign every value
No attestation, because device data are more accurate than manual entry
Review of flagged or changed values individually, with each value's source visible, before signing
items.rationale: Attestation is meaningful when it focuses the nurse on abnormal or changed values and shows where each came from. A single shift signature turns review into a rubber stamp while leaving the nurse accountable. Device data can still be wrong from artifact, placement, or the wrong patient. A co-signature on every value adds burden without targeting risk.

items.question: A hospital installs always-on ambient microphones in patient rooms to document nursing care. Which principle of the security triad is most directly at stake?
options: Availability
Integrity
Confidentiality
Non-repudiation
items.rationale: Recording everything said in a room captures protected health information from patients, visitors, and staff, so controlling who can access it is a confidentiality question. Integrity concerns whether data are accurate and unaltered, and availability whether they can be reached when needed; both matter, but less directly here. Non-repudiation is not part of the triad.

items.question: Elena Garcia scans a code at check-in, and her medication list arrives from her Medicare app. It shows lisinopril 10 mg; the chart shows 20 mg. What should the nurse do?
options: Accept the app's list, because it came from a national network
Ask Elena what she actually takes, check the pharmacy fill if needed, and document which source was used
Keep the chart's list, because it was entered by a clinician
Delete both entries and ask the provider to re-enter the medication
items.rationale: Patient-shared data is valuable but still needs reconciliation with the patient, and the chart should record the source. Neither source is automatically right: the app may be out of date and the chart may be stale. Deleting entries loses information and does not resolve the discrepancy.

items.question: According to the textbook, consumer-mediated exchange is best described as:
options: Patients accessing their own health information and sharing it with providers they choose
A query to a health information organization to locate a patient's records
A provider pushing results to another known provider
A payer sending claims data to a clearinghouse
items.rationale: Consumer-mediated exchange puts the patient in control of accessing and sharing their information. Pushing to a known provider is directed exchange, and locating records through an HIO is query-based exchange. Claims transactions are administrative, not consumer-mediated.

items.question: A nurse wants ANCC's Informatics Nursing board certification (NI-BC, formerly RN-BC). Which combination meets the practice requirement?
options: Any 30 continuing education hours and a current RN license
Five years of bedside nursing with a unit super-user role
Completion of an Epic certification sponsored by an employer
2,000 hours of informatics nursing practice in the last three years, with 30 informatics CE hours
items.rationale: ANCC requires an RN license, two years of RN practice, 30 continuing education hours in informatics within three years, and informatics practice hours, such as 2,000 hours, or 1,000 hours plus 12 graduate credits. Vendor certification and bedside experience alone do not meet the informatics practice requirement.

items.question: A staff nurse at an Epic hospital wants an Epic build certification. What is the most realistic path?
options: Buy the course and exam directly from the vendor as an individual
Complete a general health IT certificate online, which substitutes for vendor certification
Join the hospital's super-user or analyst team and seek employer sponsorship
Wait for Epic to open public enrollment after the next upgrade
items.rationale: Vendor certifications such as Epic's generally require sponsorship by an organization that uses the system, so joining the super-user or analyst track at one's employer is the usual path. Individuals generally cannot enroll on their own, and general certificates do not substitute for application-specific credentials.

items.question: In a final demonstration, a team says its tool 'saves four minutes per note.' Which answer to 'where did that number come from?' shows the strongest evidence?
options: 'That's what it felt like when we used it'
'From our baseline sheet: six synthetic cases timed with the current template and with the prototype, scored by one classmate'
'A vendor white paper reports similar savings'
'Our clinical advisor estimated it'
items.rationale: A measurable claim needs a baseline and a comparison that someone else could check. The baseline sheet ties the number to named cases and a scorer. Impressions, estimates, and vendor numbers from other settings are hypotheses, not evidence for this tool.

items.question: A team's AI draft reply to portal messages is accurate on every test case, but it appears in a separate window that the nurse opens only after she has already answered the message. Which rubric criterion does this most clearly fail?
options: Workflow problem and users (workflow fit)
Test design and baseline
Evidence and communication
Results and error analysis
items.rationale: An accurate output that arrives after the decision, in a place the user is not looking, adds work rather than removing it. That is a workflow-fit failure. More test cases, better evidence, or deeper error analysis would not fix the timing and placement.

items.question: Michalowski and colleagues (2026) describe a nursing future with no documentation burden. Based on this course's evidence, what must be true before a hospital removes manual charting of routine assessments?
options: The vendor reports high accuracy in its marketing materials
Nurses report that they like the tool in a satisfaction survey
The tool is certified by ONC
The tool is validated locally against a baseline, including omissions and subgroups, with nurses in governance and a monitored attestation process
items.rationale: The course repeatedly showed that vendor-reported performance does not guarantee local performance, that omissions are the main AI documentation error, and that oversight must be designed and measured. Satisfaction and certification matter but do not show the tool is safe for this purpose.

items.question: The textbook defines 'unintended consequences' of health IT as:
options: Errors caused only by user carelessness
Planned downtime during an upgrade
Unexpected outcomes of intentional actions, usually unfavorable, such as new types of errors after a system change
Features the vendor chose not to build
items.rationale: Houser defines unintended consequences as unexpected outcomes of intentional actions, which are typically unfavorable, such as duplicate orders caused by confusing navigation. They are not limited to user error, planned downtime, or missing features.

items.question: A pilot agent queues a potassium order on 'Liu H.', a duplicate chart for Liu Huang, because the new lab result filed there. Which enduring principle does this failure show most directly?
options: Evidence: the agent was not validated locally
Identity: automation acting on the wrong record causes faster harm
Workflow: the order arrived at the wrong time
Governance: no committee approved the pilot
items.rationale: The root failure is patient identity: an unresolved duplicate chart let a result and an automated action land on the wrong record. Validation, timing, and governance may also need attention, but identity is what failed first, and automation makes identity errors travel faster.

items.question: In 2026, federal regulators proposed cutting some health IT certification requirements while enforcing information blocking and security. What does this most likely mean for a hospital deploying AI?
options: The hospital's own governance must set and monitor more of the rules for AI use
The vendor now carries full responsibility for AI safety
AI tools no longer need clinical review
Nurses no longer need to document AI use
items.rationale: Fewer federal design mandates shift responsibility to local governance: the organization decides what AI may do, who approves, and how it is monitored. Vendors remain responsible for their products, but they do not take on the hospital's clinical accountability, and review and documentation are still needed.
